lesson_2.title: Target Search

lesson_3.title: Bubble Sort Ascending
task: Sorting improves searching efficiency[cite: 23]. Bubble Sort rearranges data by repeatedly comparing adjacent elements and swapping them if they are in the wrong order.
1. Do an outer pass over the array.
2. Run an inner loop to compare adjacent items `j` and `j+1`.
3. If the left item is larger than the right item, swap them. Heavy elements 'bubble' up to the end.
2. Nest two loops. Outer loop: `i` from 0 to length. Inner loop: `j` from 0 to length - 1.
3. If `arr[j] > arr[j+1]`, assign them swapped values (e.g., using a temp variable).
4. Return `arr`. Notice how nested loops push the time complexity to O(n²)!

lesson_3.title: Selection Sort Ascending
task: Selection Sort works by repeatedly scanning the unsorted portion of the array to find the minimum element, then swapping it with the first unsorted position[cite: 23].
1. Iterate through the array. Treat the current index `i` as the 'minimum' placeholder.
2. Scan all elements to the right of `i`.
3. If a smaller element is found, update the 'minimum' index.
4. After the inner scan completes, swap the newly found minimum element with index `i`.
2. Loop `i` from 0 to `length of arr`. Inside, set `min_idx = i`.
3. Nested loop: `j` from `i + 1` to `length of arr`. If `arr[j] < arr[min_idx]`, update `min_idx = j`.
4. Outside the inner loop, swap `arr[i]` and `arr[min_idx]`.

lesson_3.title: Visual Sort Tracking
task: Instead of fully sorting the array, let's observe exactly what happens after a *single pass* of Bubble Sort. This hands-on approach helps build tangible mental models of the algorithm's execution[cite: 23].
1. Do not use an outer pass loop. Only use a single loop to scan through the array once.
2. Compare `arr[j]` with `arr[j+1]`. Swap if the left is larger.
3. By the end of this single pass, the absolute largest number will have 'bubbled' to the very last index.
4. Return `arr`. Notice how removing the outer loop drops the complexity back down to O(n) Linear Time!
